**Answer: Yes, $\mu \geq 0$.**

**Proof.**

Recall that a Radon measure $\nu$ on $\Omega$ is non-negative (i.e. $\nu \geq 0$) if and only if
$$\int_\Omega \phi \, d\nu \geq 0 \quad \text{for every } \phi \in C_0(\Omega) \text{ with } \phi \geq 0.$$
(The forward direction is immediate from the definition of a non-negative measure; the reverse direction follows because if $\nu$ assigned negative mass to some Borel set, one could approximate its indicator by compactly supported continuous functions and obtain a negative integral — equivalently, this is the standard positivity criterion from the Riesz–Markov representation theorem.)

Now let $\phi \in C_0(\Omega)$ be arbitrary with $\phi \geq 0$. By hypothesis each $\mu_n$ is non-negative, so
$$\int_\Omega \phi \, d\mu_n \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } n.$$
By weak-* convergence $\mu_n \rightharpoonup^* \mu$, the sequence of real numbers
$$a_n := \int_\Omega \phi \, d\mu_n$$
converges to
$$a := \int_\Omega \phi \, d\mu.$$
A limit of non-negative real numbers is non-negative, so
$$\int_\Omega \phi \, d\mu = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_\Omega \phi \, d\mu_n \geq 0.$$
Since this holds for every non-negative $\phi \in C_0(\Omega)$, the positivity criterion above yields $\mu \geq 0$.

**Remark.** No additional hypothesis (uniform boundedness of total masses, absolute continuity, etc.) is needed for the conclusion $\mu \geq 0$. The weak-* limit of non-negative measures is always non-negative, because positivity is tested against non-negative continuous compactly supported functions, and non-negativity is preserved under pointwise limits of real sequences. (Uniform boundedness of $\{\mu_n(\Omega)\}$ would be required only to guarantee that a weak-* limit *exists* as a finite Radon measure; here existence of $\mu$ is already assumed.)

### PROOF COMPLETE

Yes. For any non-negative $\phi \in C_0(\Omega)$, $\int \phi d\mu_n \geq 0$, so the limit $\int \phi d\mu \geq 0$. By Riesz representation / positivity characterization, $\mu \geq 0$.
